prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 407px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 62px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 61px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r1B: widths [103, 80, 80, 80, 80] · table 424×813px · row heights [60, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 3 · OVERFLOWS the box by 64px
Design r1C: widths [103, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 440×790px · row heights [36, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 80px
Design r2A: widths [176, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 513×487px · row heights [36, 83, 36, 106, 60, 83, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 153px
Design r2B: widths [224, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 561×394px · row heights [36, 60, 36, 83, 60, 60, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 201px
Design r2C: widths [150, 86, 86, 86, 86] · table 495×557px · row heights [36, 83, 60, 129, 83, 83, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 135px
Design r3A: widths [104, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 441×790px · row heights [36, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 81px
Design r3B: widths [128, 84, 84, 84, 84] · table 465×604px · row heights [36, 106, 60, 129, 83, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 105px
Design r3C: widths [120, 83, 84, 83, 85] · table 456×673px · row heights [36, 129, 83, 129, 83, 106, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 96px

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r2A"],"acceptable":["r2C","r3B","r3C"],"bad":[{"design":"r1B","why":"The 80px data columns force 4/5 headers to wrap and cause three mid-word splits, breaking values such as $318.4M into separate lines and destroying numeric comparability."},{"design":"r1C","why":"The 103px metric column collapses long row labels into 5–6-line word stacks, making the table 790px tall while the numeric columns sit mostly empty; rows stop reading as phrases."},{"design":"r3A","why":"Essentially the same fault as r1C: a 104px metric column produces one-word-per-line row headers and excessive vertical sprawl for a table whose data cells are short."},{"design":"r2B","why":"The 224px metric column over-prioritizes labels; at 360px only one full year column is visible, so comparing years requires repeated horizontal scrolling and the row header scrolls away."}],"contrast":null,"ranges":[[168,190],[83,88],[83,89],[83,88],[84,90]],"rationale":"This is a row-header comparison table: the metric column carries phrases, while the four year columns are interchangeable numeric roles. r2A gives the metric column enough width to keep labels to 2–4 lines and gives each year column just enough width to keep headers and values such as $318.4M intact, producing a compact 487px-tall table with a clear roughly 2:1 hierarchy. It overflows by 153px, but the alternatives either force one-word-per-line row labels or push so much of the year series off-screen that comparison becomes cumbersome. r1B is clearly unacceptable because its narrow data columns split numeric identifiers and wrap headers.","principles":{"general":["Size a row-header column by the longest natural phrase it must carry; equal widths across all columns usually misallocate space.","For numeric or date columns, set width from the longest unbreakable token plus padding; below that, values and headers split and the table loses integrity.","On narrow screens, horizontal overflow can be the lesser evil, but only if the row header plus enough comparable data columns remain visible; otherwise comparison breaks.","Avoid tall, sparse rows created by one-word-per-line wrapping; a wider label column often buys more scanning speed than it costs in overflow."],"specific":["The minimum no-split width here is about 440px (103 + 4×84), so every valid design must overflow 360px; the real choice is how much extra width to trade for shorter rows.","The four year columns need about 84px each; 80px splits values and headers, while 86–90px adds little.","The metric column needs roughly 168–190px to avoid the 5–6-line word stacks seen at 103–120px.","r2A's 176px metric column is the best balance; r2B's 224px is too wide for the comparative task."]},"tradeoffs":"Horizontal scrolling versus vertical height: r1C/r3A keep three year columns visible initially but make rows very tall, while r2A accepts fewer visible years for readable labels and compact rows. Some designers may prefer r3B's smaller 105px overflow over r2A's 153px.","uncertain":"Exact range boundaries depend on browser line-breaking; whether r2B is publishable inside a horizontally scrollable container; whether r1C/r3A should be treated as bad or merely as an acceptable no-split fallback; whether the first column would remain sticky during horizontal scroll."}
